newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Reserve Bank alters bank investment norms.
newsitem.headline: India's Reserve Bank alters bank investment norms.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on Tuesday removed a 5.0 percent limit on banks' investments of their incremental deposits in bonds, debentures and preference shares.
The central bank said the limit would be applicable only to ordinary shares of companies, including state-run firms.

"It has now been decided to exclude from this limit investments in preference shares, debentures, bonds of private corporate bodies," the central bank said in its monetary policy statement for the first six months of 1997/98 (April-March).
"In other words, the limit will be applicable for investments in ordinary shares of corporates, including public sector units," RBI said.
"We are now saying that banks can invest up to 5.0 percent of their additional deposits in shares," RBI governor Chakravarty Rangarajan told Reuters Television in an interview.
RBI said money lent to companies against shares as the firms waited for capital to be raised through a public issue would be included in this 5.0 percent limit.
"We are also allowing banks to lend to corporates against shares held by them to enable them to meet promoters' contribution to the equity of new companies," Rangarajan said.
The proposals do not require any further approvals but the RBI said details of the changed norms would be communicated to banks.
